utterances.text: Yes. You mean people who didn't have citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, people who didn't have Bosnian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were considered to be foreign nationals, foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who [as interpreted] the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Sefer Halilovic of the day was born, for example?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can I give you the answer? Was it Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can I suggest an answer?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either. I really don't know. I can't say. Possibly. Sefer Halilovic, you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know where the province of Sandzak is located?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So a person born in Sandzak, was it somebody who was not a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina then but the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And he wasn't the only one. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if an individual born in Serbia had permanent residence in Croatia, would that person be considered a foreigner, a foreign national from the viewpoint of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, since you don't know about your commander, were there people who were not commanders, who were ordinary soldiers, combatants, fighters, were there a large number of those at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, if you look at this article -- or let me ask you this first. Did you know in 1992 and 1993 that a large number of members, that is to say citizens of the former SFRY born in Sandzak, born in Kosovo, born in Croatia, for example, found themselves to be among the ranks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is common knowledge. It is something that is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Karic, in view of this fact the article stipulated, in your opinion, who did this article apply to?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know we had the problem you have mentioned, especially in the 1st Corps of the BH Army. In Sarajevo, there really were a lot of people who had come to Sarajevo, they had all the official documents mentioning the place of birth, Sandzak, Kosovo, et cetera, et cetera, and there were people who weren't citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they joined the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes your testimony, Mr. Karic. Thank you for having spent a number of days in The Hague to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel, the Prosecution, and the Judges. We wish you a good trip home, and we wish you all the best in your professional career, in your company. I'll now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another witness. I'll take this opportunity to give some documents to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I'd first like to make sure that you're receiving interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You'll have to take the solemn declaration. But before you do so, could you approach the microphones, please. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my name is Ferid Jasarevic. I was born on the 15th of October, 1950 in the village of Jezerci in Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession? Do you receive a salary? What do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the moment I work as a teacher in a primary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind? And if so, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, in May, I joined the BH Army, and I was a member of the army until the 19th of November 1993 when I was given a work obligation, and I started working as a teacher in a primary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me what unit you were a part of until November 1993, and did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until November 1993, I was a member of the 306th Brigade. And I didn't have a rank of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were just a private, then. Did you have any particular duties to perform within the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the 306th Brigade, I was a member of the sector for morale. Husic Halim, the assistant commander for morale, was my superior, and I was in the -- an officer in the 306th Brigade in the sector for morale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in November 1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've never testified before a court before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. To ensure that everything runs smoothly and to avoid wasting any time, I would like to provide you with some information on the procedure that will be followed. This is what I do whenever a witness appears before the Chamber. You will first have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel. Counsel for the accused, whom you have certainly met, are to your left. They will conduct what we call the examination-in-chief. The questions they put to you must not be leading. The questions put to you will be neutral. After this state has been completed, the Prosecution, who are sitting to your right -- who are sitting to your right, will also ask you questions. They will take up just as much time as the Defence took. This is what we call the cross-examination. The party cross-examining is allowed to put questions that are leading. And this is what makes it different from examination-in-chief. Try to provide clear answers to the questions put to you by both parties because the Judges don't have any written documents that relate to the testimony you will be giving. This is why your answers are so important. If you fail to understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. In addition, the Judges before you, and usually there are three of us but one is absent for professional reasons, the Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions at any point in time. As a rule, the Judges ask questions after both parties have concluded their questions. And the parties may ask a witness questions after the Judges put questions to the witness. But if you answer all the questions, it won't be necessary for the Judges to ask you any questions. I should also point out two other factors: Given the fact that you are a former member of the 306th Brigade, you have taken the solemn declaration. This means that you are no longer a witness of either of the parties. You are a witness who will be testifying in the interests of justice. And this means that you are obliged to speak the truth. As a teacher, you're aware of the fact that sanctions can be imposed in the case of false testimony. Such sanctions could include a prison sentence. Secondly, I would like to point out that when answering a question, a witness might feel that his answer might provide information that could be used in a subsequent prosecution against that witness. According to our Rules, the witness can refuse to answer the question. In such a case, the Trial Chamber can oblige the witness to answer the question, but if that is the case, the witness is granted a form of immunity, which means that whatever the witness says can't be used against the witness. This rule allows witnesses to speak the truth. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. If you feel there are any difficulties, do inform us of the fact. We will try to resolve them. Usually, the hearing goes on for an hour and a half, and then we have a break for technical reasons, after which we resume the hearing. But since it's now already five to 12.00, we will continue until half past 12.00, and we will then have to have our break for technical reasons, and then we will resume at about five to 1.00. Without wasting any more time, I will give the floor to the Defence who will provide you with a little additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the Presiding Judge has just told you, I would like to ask you to briefly pause after I put a question to you since we speak the same language. My questions have to be interpreted so that everyone in the courtroom can follow what is being said. And this is why I'd be grateful if you could pause after I have put a question to you before answering. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already said, Mr. Jasarevic, that you are a teacher. Could you tell us something about your educational background. Which schools did you complete, where, and when?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Han Bila in Travnik Municipality. I completed secondary school for teachers in Travnik in 1970. I studied teacher training. And since then, I have been working as a teacher. I work with children in the first four classes of primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, tell me, which areas have you worked in -- or which areas did you work in and in which schools did you work before the war?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I started working in 1970. But I have always worked in the Mehurici primary school. I still work in that school. There was a break in 1972 when I was in the JNA, and also there was a break from 1992 to 1993 when I was a member of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You already said that you were an officer in the sector for moral guidance in the 306th Brigade. Mr. Jasarevic, could you tell me, when you joined the defence, did the 306th Brigade exist at that time? Or did you join some other defence units?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I joined the BH Army in May 1992. At the time, the 306th Brigade did not exist. It was a problem to organise defence. So the Territorial Defence sector staff in Mehurici was formed. It included Jezerci, Fazlici, Zavidovici [phoen], Bozerce [phoen], Zabrdje, et cetera. We organised companies or units in the villages, or platoons; it depended on the size of the village. Our commander was in Mehurici. The sector staff was our command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, did the Territorial Defence sector staff obtain a different name? Was it given a different name? Did you form detachments or formations of a similar kind?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, since the situation was becoming increasingly complex, we had to organise ourselves as best as possible in a military sense. So detachments were formed, and I think there were three detachments. There was the Mehurici detachment, the Luta Greda [phoen] detachment, and I think there was a detachment called the Krpeljici detachment. I can't remember whether there was a Han Bila detachment. I think there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, which detachment were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do go ahead. You do have to make such lengthy pauses. I hope that the interpreters will have time to translate brief questions.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Mehurici detachment which was in the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, who was your detachment commander?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the commander was Fahir Camdzic. I'll repeat this, the commander of our detachment was Fahir Camdzic, Fahir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, what kind of weapons did you have when you joined the sector staff and later the Mehurici detachment?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you about the weapons that we had in my village. For example, my village didn't have weapons of any kind. My village is a small one. It has about 400 inhabitants. We had six hunting rifles. We had one automatic rifle which a policeman lent us. We had two pistols. Those were the weapons my village had. So at the beginning, as you can see, we had no weapons of any kind. That's all we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, did Croatian inhabitants from that area join Territorial Defence units? Or to be more specific, do you know which units were joined by the Croatian population? And do you know how they joined these units?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: A minor number of Croats joined the BH Army. I know that two Croats from my village joined the Territorial Defence. Later it was to be called the BH Army. And the other able-bodied inhabitants joined the HVO at the very beginning. They were not members of the BH Army. There were very few of them who were. Most of the able-bodied Croats joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you have just told us about the weapons you had. How were the HVO units armed and equipped in your area?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The HVO units were far superior in terms of weapons and uniforms. They had the most modern equipment, the most modern weapons, automatic rifles. They had what we called camouflage uniforms. They were well trained. They had good footwear. They had everything that a soldier needed to have at the time in comparison to the members of the Territorial Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the 306th Brigade was formed, you said that you were in the -- you were an official in the sector for moral guidance, and Mr. Husic was your superior, or rather, he was the assistant commander for moral guidance. Could you tell me where the headquarters of the brigade command was located at the time and where was your workplace located and your military place of work, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the brigade command was in Rudnik, and my workplace, my military workplace was in Rudnik, in the offices of the Rudnik building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the 306th Brigade have any barracks where its members were billeted? And if it didn't have any such barracks, where were they when they weren't at their combat positions?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The 306th Brigade didn't have barracks of any kind. They didn't have any buildings of its own. The soldiers would spend their free time at home. They weren't billeted in barracks. They returned home when they left their combat positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, as a member of one of the organs of the brigade command, where would you be when you weren't at your workplace or when you weren't carrying out any of your military duties?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: When I wasn't carrying out military duties of any kind, I would return to my village. And we farmed there. We would grow potatoes, beans, carrots. The situation was difficult, so that's how we fed ourselves. That food enabled us to survive. So I spent my free time in the village where I farmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, until when did you remain performing duties in the organ for moral guidance? And did you assume any other duties? And if so, what kind of duties did you assume?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the organ for moral guidance until the 19th of November, 1993. As I said, I was an official in the organ for moral guidance. At some time in August 1993, in the sector for moral guidance, I was the chief -- I became the chief of the social service within that military hierarchy. Within the sector for morale and religious guidance, a social service was formed, and I became the chief, and I had an assistant. We were responsible for social care for soldiers and their families. I'd also like to point out that for a brief period of time, from the 19th or the 18th of June - I can't remember the exact date - up until mid-August, pursuant to an order from the commander, I was transferred to the Luta Greda forward command post northwest of Mehurici at the lines facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. As you can see, I was involved in moral guidance at all times, but my duties varied because sometimes the situation was such that I had to do what my superior would order me to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In November 1993, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: In November 1993, conditions were such that it was possible for schools to function. So I returned to my job, and I did what I have always done and what I still do. In wartime conditions, I taught children with my colleagues, children who were in the first four classes of primary school. I worked in Velika Bukovica, which is about nine kilometres north of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us about the duties you had in that organ for moral guidance, the duties you had before you became involved in social care for soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The duties I had in the sector -- in the organ for moral guidance as an official for moral and religious guidance, I had the following duties: We had to be concerned with the moral of the combatants. We informed the combatants of the international laws and rules on how to fight and how to treat wounded men. So we had to take care of combatants' moral. But given the situation we were in, we were always involved in social affairs since the main issue concerns how a soldier can get involved in combat if he has a family that's hungry. So we had to ensure that their family members were not hungry. So these were some of the main tasks we had in the organ for moral guidance. As far as religious affairs are concerned, I didn't get involved in that very much since the assistant commander for moral, Husic Halim, was a specialist in that field. He had completed a religious school in Sarajevo. And he was concerned with those affairs as far as the soldiers are concerned. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Jasarevic, under the prevailing conditions, how far was your job linked to the needs for establishing lines of command or chains of command as soldiers like to put it? Or rather, how far was it linked to bringing the population into the army? And did you encounter any problems in that respect?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were, of course, problems. There were serious problems with regard to organisation. Firstly, because the Territorial Defence which had functioned up until then was disbanded to all intents and purposes, and so the units of Territorial Defence, as we said, included Bosniak Muslims mostly. So the first problem was lack of men, and we had to make up for this lack of men by having more than one shift or we had -- we didn't have enough men. But we managed to do our -- what we could to defend ourselves during that period of time. The problem of command, or control and command, well, the soldiers weren't properly trained at the beginning. And people weren't ready to take the decision to go to the front lines because, of course, they could have been killed there. But later on, people realised that they had this duty and they performed that duty. There were less problems once the brigade had been established, of course. And after that, the problems decreased.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Jasarevic, what relations did you have with the civilian organs working in the same area? What was your relationship with them?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: In the area that I worked in, or rather, where my brigade was operative, or more precisely, the moral guidance and religious affairs sector, there were local communities and communes who had their presidents and representatives, and then there was the civilian protection or civil defence organs. And we took care of the soldiers through the moral guidance department, and we managed to coordinate with the civilian authorities. And they, according to their possibilities, provided the families in the villages with what they could and in that way saw to it that they weren't left to go hungry. So among other things, this was one of the ways of communicating with the civilian authorities in the local communes, and they were representatives and presidents of the local commune. And within the civilian defence there was civil protection, defence, and so on. So via the moral guidance department we sought to help the families of the soldiers, of the combatants.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At a given point in time, were you in a superior position to the civilian authorities and their organs, whether it was organs of power and authority, the civilian police force, or civilian protection? So was the 306th Brigade in actual fact at one point, did it take over complete power and authority, and was it superior and placed above the organs of civilian power and authority?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, never, not at any time was our command superior to the civilian authorities. There was no need for that because as I said, the civilian authorities existed. All we did was to coordinate our work. As an official in charge of moral guidance, et cetera, we would contact the organs of power and authority in the local communes when a matter arose that needed coordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Jasarevic, at some point in time, did you happen to notice that in the area of the Bila Valley, some foreigners from African and Asian countries had begun to appear?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: While the regional staff existed before the brigade was established, I arrived in Mehurici one day to the regional staff there, and I was told that some men had come to the school, Arabs, Africans, but I didn't know what their goal and intention was. I learned at the time -- I don't remember the date, but when I came to Mehurici, I learned that some people had indeed arrived there and they had been put up in the floor above. The regional staff was down below on the ground floor, and I assume that these others were on the floor up, the upper storey.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where these people came from, where they were coming from, and did you learn later on what role they appeared there in? What role they played when they came? What their role was there?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the BH Army myself and as an ordinary individual, I had no official information as to who these people were. The information I gained was only in talking to my neighbours. And I learned in talking to my neighbours that they had mostly come in from Arab countries, Iraq and Jordan, and that there were some Arab humanitarians who had come in to help the local population. And at the beginning, they handed out some packages, parcels, I don't know. But they called themselves humanitarians, Arab humanitarians. Later on, I learned that they should have -- or rather, people said that they were called Mujahedin. And that was the accepted term.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you're a teacher yourself. What did you know about the Mujahedins until then? What did you know about them?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am a teacher, and I try to keep abreast of world events. I read the papers every day. I have a religious background as well, but I never actually had heard about the concept of Mujahedin up until then and what it actually denoted and what they were and what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen at one time when these foreigners, these Mujahedin, changed the place of their sojourn? And do you know where they came to be located, where they set up residence?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were in the school building up until the arrival of the 1st Detachment, the 1st Battalion in actual fact of the 306th Brigade. They lived a little freer. They would imbibe alcohol. They sang. And they couldn't make contact with them. So I suppose they left and set up a camp in Poljanice, in the abandoned Serb houses. So they left in actual fact when the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade moved into the school building. Let me also say that their activities in the beginning were exclusively humanitarian, but later on, gradually, they tried to establish contact with the local population. And then they went to the mosques and held religious teaching there. They told the people that they should pray to God differently than they had been doing up until then. The people reacted to this, and there was antagonism between them and the local population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the local population at that period, and we're talking about 1993, in the Bila Valley, were there people, inhabitants who had come in from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the local population, there were a lot of people coming in from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I would like to mention firstly people from the neighbouring communes, such as Kotor Varos, Siprage, and so on from the northwest, and they became members of the BH Army. They joined the BH Army. I apologise, in Han Bila, there was a transit point because there were too many refugees. Some would come to Han Bila. Others would be sent further on to Zenica, but there were a lot of people from the Krajina, mostly from the Krajina. And as I said, from the neighbouring Kotor Varos Municipality. When I say the Krajina, I meant that the area where in fact the Serb and Montenegrin aggressors had occupied, expelling the local population from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Jasarevic, in addition to the 306th Brigade, which is as you've said was established on the -- in the area of the Bila Valley and when its headquarters and command in Rudnik, the local population and the other displaced population, did they mobilise fighters for other brigades of the BH Army as well?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, in view of the enormous influx of people coming in from Krajina and the neighbouring commune, other brigades were established. But let me say first that of the local population, or a part of the local population led to problems of organisation because they didn't wish to join up with the 306th Brigade. They were people from Gluha Bukovica, for example, and Zabrdje. They were members. They became members of the 314th Brigade in actual fact. And apart from that, there another battalion of the 306th Brigade made up of men belonging to the Siprage Municipality before the war. And they formed this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The important thing is that you've explained to us that it wasn't only the local population that joined up with the 306th Brigade. Now, tell me, please, Mr. Jasarevic, and you began talking about the foreigners who set up a camp in Poljanice and their relationship to the population. Did you happen to notice that these foreigners began to change their customs? And in addition -- and conduct? And in addition to the humanitarian work that they were engaged in, that they began engaging in if I can put it military activities? Did you have any knowledge to that effect?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: After their humanitarian activities and the work they did to give religious training and instruction, they began to engage in military activities, too. At first, we would see them wearing their national dress. But later on, they would put on military uniforms, camouflage uniforms. But sometimes even over their camouflage uniforms, they would wear their national costume, their national dress. But their activity boiled down to the fact that in their own units they would try and recruit some young people and train them militarily, to give them military training. And in return, the people that underwent training with them would be issued rifles. So some of these military-able young men would join up with these people to be trained, to obtain rifles, and then they would go back to their own original unit or would join up with some other unit. So that was the kind of activity, the military activity they engaged in at the beginning, to the best of my knowledge, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, did those foreigners ever belong to the 306th Brigade? Or to the best of your knowledge, were they ever resubordinated to the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: According to my knowledge as an official and clerk in the department, and what I was able to see on the ground, the members of the El Mujahed were never in the 306th Brigade, nor where they resubordinated to it, nor did they wish to be subordinated or attached to it. So they were not -- the Mujahid never belonged to the 306th Brigade. Quite the contrary. Since you're asking me, I can tell you that as the command at the beginning, there was a certain amount of antagonism because they didn't wish to cooperate with us. So in a way, we were disillusioned with them. And they had all kinds of food. They had all kinds of food on the floor up above us, whereas we had to make do with lentils and beans. So not only were they not members of the 306th Brigade, but we were never able to establish any kind of contact, nor did they help us in any way or assist us in any way. And they were not members of the 306th Brigade. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Now, these HVO units to which the Croatian population was mobilised, can you tell me where they were deployed?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, the Territorial Defence units secured the lines facing the Chetnik and Serb aggressor at Mount Vlasic. There were no HVO troops with us. They were probably deployed in their own villages. And then afterwards, they started to set up checkpoints. They were mostly along the roads. And later on, they were on important elevations and features above the Bosnian villages. So that is where they were. And I know that their headquarters, the brigade headquarters were -- what was the brigade's name? I can't remember. But it was at Guca Gora. And they were in their own villages and along the various checkpoints on features above the Bosnian villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The position assumed by the HVO on dominant features and elevation points as you said, did it lead to certain problems? Did it create problems for you as assistant commander for moral guidance, for example, in explaining to the soldiers why they were entrenching and fortifying themselves rather than going to defend the area facing the Serb forces, for instance?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, it was a very great problem, a major problem how to explain to the soldiers what was going on because people who were our allies until yesterday had suddenly changed face and left us and were waging a military policy of their own, if I could put it that way. There was an about turn. So at the beginning, they didn't prevent us from going to the front line. Later on they did. They started preventing our units engaged in holding the lines facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. They didn't let them pass. And we had problems with moral guidance and morale generally. We received orders from the superior command to begin with that we should not enter into any conflicts with the HVO, but that we should also -- always try to solve our differences peacefully because we had to build up a state with them and we had to free Bosnia-Herzegovina by joining forces with them. That was difficult to explain to the ordinary rank-and-file soldier, but we did adhere to those instructions, and we didn't enter into a conflict, although they were often superior in equipment and materiel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps this is a good time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 12.30. We're going to break and reconvene at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, before the break, we were talking about some problems with the HVO. Tell me now, please, whether you, too, were one of the victims of excessive incidents and situations, an attack launched by the HVO, in fact.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Under such conditions, I myself could not have been spared humiliation. It was very bad. I'll just mention two incidents which are characteristic. Sometime at the beginning of May, end of April at the Okoka [phoen] junction, we were in a bus driving to Travnik, and a checkpoint there, and the HVO stopped the bus quite simply, told all the Muslims to get out, and we had to go on on foot. It was a terrible humiliation for us, but we had no other choice. The second instance of humiliation was experienced by myself and my co-fighters of the 306th Brigade. I think it was in May, while we were returning from a work assignment at Rudnik, towards our house, towards Mehurici. Near Mehurici, some masked HVO soldiers intercepted us. They told us to get out of the van. They swore at us and forced us to lie face down on the ground on our stomachs, and they told us to graze, to eat grass. And then they went from one soldier to the next, confiscating all their valuables, or rather what they had on them, a pistol, I think one of them had a rifle. And they took the trainers, sneakers off one of them. I heard a shot at that point. And I felt -- thought they would kill me. I would have suffered death more easily than being taken off to a camp in Busovaca or anything like that. But when they searched us and took the items that they wanted, they left us alone and went back to their own homes. I didn't reach the command post at Rudnik. So those are those two instances of humiliation, humiliating behaviour that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This kind of conduct on the part of the HVO, their conduct to the army and the command, did it lead the brigade into a situation in which, or rather the command into a situation in which it was unable to rally its ranks? And do you know, for example, where at the end of May and beginning of June the command of the 306th Brigade was actually located? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: After that unfortunate event, I and my fellow fighters weren't able to go to Rudnik any more, so we reported to Mehurici which is where the headquarters of the 1st Battalion was. And part of the command was in Mehurici, and I'm just going to mention the names I remember. There was Munir Karic, Kasim Music and myself, and some other people from logistics but I can't remember them all. We stayed there and tried to establish communication as far as was possible and to go about our affairs in keeping with the provisions and duties imposed on us at that time. The second part of the command was in Krpeljici. I'll mention the names I remember. There was commander Asim Semic [phoen], the assistant for moral guidance, Husic Halim, and one of the battalion commanders, Fahir Camdzic was his name, and I don't remember who else was there. At the HQ at Rudnik, Husic remained there. What was his first name? Arif Husic, yes. And Asim Delalic. So those two men stayed there. And that's how we were able to function, from these sort of provisional places in Guca Gora and Rudnik and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that the blockades had been set up and the conduct of the HVO was what it was that the command had been dispersed, can you tell us the situation that the members of the 306th Brigade found themselves in and whether it was possible to communicate between and among the places in the Bila Dolina where they lived, Bila Valley where they lived? Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was just waiting for a pause. No communication was possible because at all the important points, the HVO had set up their checkpoints. I'll enumerate just some of them. The Lagev [phoen] checkpoint, that was the first checkpoint as you go from Mehurici. The Guca Gora checkpoint towards Travnik, the Putic checkpoint. And they would stop people passing by. They confiscated any items they wanted. And afterwards they didn't allow anybody to pass by. The next checkpoint was towards Stala Bila, and it wasn't possible to communicate with Zenica either which was equidistant from Travnik. There was an HVO checkpoint at Ovnak. So faced with that situation, the fighters were not able to respond and report to their units' positions, but stayed in the villages where they did their best to perform their military assignments as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, in a situation of that kind which you have just described to us, and when you yourself stayed on in Mehurici due to force of circumstance, did news reach Mehurici about a possible attack, about possible attacks launched by the HVO? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what I remember of those times, and this is what happened. Refugees were coming in from Vitez and the surrounding villages where the HVO had already started their cleansing operations of the Bosnian population in the surrounding villages, Gacice, for example, Veceriska, Grbavica, and the town Vitez, the town of Vitez itself. After that, refugees came in from Radojcici, Bandol and places like that. And then we learned about a terrible occurrence, a terrible crime that had been committed at Bukovica where members of the Croatian Defence Council had surrounded the village and massacred the civilian population, that they even set fire to some people in a garage and killed them. I don't know how many. But this news reached the HQ that there were a lot of wounded, and that a lot of people had been killed, 9 or 10 of them, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you were in the command of the 1st Battalion yourself, tell me, please, whether you know what happened on the 8th of June, 1993, for example.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: After we had found out that a crime in Bukovica had been committed, an attempt was made to assist members of the BH Army who were in that sector. Camdzic Fahir, the commander with his unit from Krpeljici -- well, they couldn't break through because of the blockade by the HVO. They tried to get to Vlasic, to get to Bukovica. But this wasn't possible because HVO forces were located there. I think the area was called Kosoric. I don't know exactly. So it wasn't possible to assist those people in Bukovica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, although you weren't involved in military planning and organisation, do you know whether parts of the 306th Brigade nevertheless went to assist members of the 306th in Gornja Bukovica? And do you know which route BH Army units used?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't have enough information about that, but as far as I can remember, an attempt was made. It wasn't possible to go over Vlasic and Krpeljici, but an attempt was made to go in the direction of Radonjici and Maline. They tried to break through the defence lines. They tried to break through the lines of the HVO in that area. That's when I heard some shooting, and I don't know what happened then. I didn't have the information. There were no communications, and as an official I didn't have any other information about how this operation was proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an army member and as an official for moral guidance, on the 8th of June, were you faced with the fact that some people were being brought to Mehurici? And on that day or on subsequent days, did you receive an order of any kind from your superior?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, well, it's a day I remember quite well. First of all, Bosniak refugees inundated the area, and I don't know at what time but civilians arrived, civilians who had been transferred from Maline to Mehurici. They had been transferred by combatants of the 1st Battalion. Apparently they had asked the BH Army to protect them. They did so. They tried to protect those people. So some Croatian civilians, women and children, arrived in Mehurici. And they were placed in the sports hall. I haven't fully answered your question. I apologise. There was an unusual situation. On that day, I wasn't given an order from my superiors. It was only on the following day that the assistant commander for morale, my superior, gave me an order. Since I had already been in contact with the civilian authorities, I was ordered to try to coordinate action with the civilian authorities, with the civilian protection and to provide those people with assistance, to see what could be done through me and through the BH Army. I was to try and make sure that the conditions were acceptable for them. So I immediately contacted the chief of civilian protection. He agreed to cooperate, and we tried to provide them with blankets and other material, with all of the blankets and other material that we had, so that the children and old people could use them. We tried to provide them with the same amount of food as the amount provided to other refugees. So those civilians in the sports hall had just -- had the same things that others had, other refugees had.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: (Redacted) We tried to do what we thought was best for them. What happened happened, and I would have done everything I could have done to protect those people. I think that we managed to do this to a certain extent, and I think that we saved their lives, which is what was most important at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From that point in time when you established contact with the civilian protection and the civilian authorities, who ensured that those people had everything they needed in terms of food and other necessary items that they required, given the conditions they were living in and given the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The civilian protection took care of this, and I as a member of the BH Army, who happened to be there and I had certain experience. I tried to help them, to coordinate action, so the civilian protection in the Mehurici local commune helped them the most. And the policemen from the Ministry of the Interior provided security for them. So there were quite secure. Their lives were not under threat. And they had food. Perhaps not enough, but enough to survive. That was the case for the other refugees of Bosniak nationality. So the civilian protection took care of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just a minute. Could the Registrar prepare an order to redact from page 71, line 5 a name that appears there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to draw your attention to that fact. Mr. President, perhaps lines 3 to 8 should be redacted since these lines might reveal the identity of the person concerned, and that person had been granted full protective measures when testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, prepare an order to redact what appears in the transcript from line 3 to line 8. I'd also like to point out that in response to a question put by you, he mentioned the name of a person from the civilian protection with whom he had contact. I heard him refer to this person in his own language, but the name does not appear in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you please repeat the name of the person with whom you had contact in the Mehurici civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The person whom I contacted in Mehurici civilian protection is called Selava Kasim. Selava Kasim. He was an inhabitant of Mehurici, and he still lives there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, could you tell me whether you at any time tried to establish contact with the Red Cross or did you try to do this immediately so they could visit these civilians? And as far as you know, did such a visit ever take place?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My superior and I were obliged to inform the international organisations as soon as possible, and above all the Red Cross, so that they could come and see what sort of conditions the people were living in and so that they could register the people and participate in providing them with assistance. I think in eight or ten days' time we managed to organise this. International Red Cross people came to Mehurici. They visited the people, the civilians, the women and children in the sports hall. They registered these people. And while I was there, they had no objections to raise about their accommodation. They just observed the situation, made a record of what they had seen, and I think that to a certain extent, they were satisfied with the way in which these people had been treated, as far as I know. So in about ten days' time, they came and registered them. This was a task that we carried out as a matter of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, from your body for moral guidance and together with you and the civilian protection, were there any other individuals who assisted the civilian authorities when carrying out their tasks and in order to enable them to carry out their tasks as best as possible?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was also a representative from the moral sector whose name was Music, Kasim. Since I see there are errors when names are mentioned, I'll repeat this name, Music Kasim. In my absence, he did the same sort of duties I did. His role was identical to the one I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, did you stay on in Mehurici until these civilians left the sports hall, or were you given a different task in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: When civilians left, I wasn't there because my commander assigned me a different task. Music Kasim, my colleague, was present when they left, but I wasn't. I was involved in another task. The command had ordered me to go to the forward command post called Parica Greda which is on Vlasic facing the Serbian and Montenegrin lines. During that period, that two-month period, I was present up there, up until the second half of August I would say, and my tasks were quite different at the time. They had nothing to do with what I have already mentioned. And as far as the events in that region down there are concerned, I knew nothing because my duties were quite different, so I couldn't say anything about that period since I was absent for two months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you returned from the combat positions after two months, tell me, what sort of duties did you then perform?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: When I had carried out my task up there, I received another order appointing me as chief of the social service in the 306th Brigade. Naturally, all this was within the sector for moral guidance. My superior was still Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, did you then come across any problems concerning accommodation for troops, and were there any other problems concerning social assistance for their families and refugees in that area?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, we weren't responsible for the refugees, apart from members for -- of the BH Army. That was our only responsibility. Naturally, we had lots of problems. There was a total blockade. Everyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina will remember 1993 as a year in which everyone's fighting for survival. There was no food. There was nothing. And the combatants had to go to the lines. They had to leave their families behind. They were hungry. So again, we tried to coordinate action with the civilian authorities and the municipality and with the local civilian authorities, so we could enable these people to live a normal life to a certain extent. There was a period when it was necessary to have at least a little flour, and then the people would be happy. That meant they would survive. As far as accommodation is concerned, there were a lot of problems. As I said, the soldiers didn't have their own premises where units could -- to which units could return after a combat operation. Instead, the troops had to return to their homes, to their villages, and that is where they spent their free time doing agricultural work, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, since your brigade troops were recruited from the Bila region, and you said there was combat action in Bandol, Velika Bukovica and in other areas, could you tell me, after these combat operations, who remained or what remained in those villages? Bandol and Velika Bukovica, what sort of a state did they remain in? What happened to the troops from those places?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Bandol and Velika Bukovica were burned down to the ground. That's what I was told by the soldiers who went there and then returned. That's what they said. I didn't go there myself. But that's -- they did burn it to the ground. The mosque in Bandol was also destroyed. All the houses in Bukovica were also torched when the HVO launched its attack. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, when you were involved in this social work, did you notice a Croatian village that had been totally destroyed and torched in the way that Bandol and Velika Bukovica had been destroyed and torched?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning when I was down there for that two-month period, up until November, I couldn't notice anything like that. All the houses were intact at the beginning. Perhaps stables had burned down in Radonjici or Guca Gora. I did notice such things. But the houses in the Croatian villages were intact, at least during the period that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. At the moment, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here in the courtroom, we represent the Prosecution in this case. I have just a few questions for you, sir. Let me ask you about a couple of things you've testified about this morning. You mentioned the events in Bandol and Velika Bukovica and the humiliations that you and other soldiers in the 306th Brigade suffered at HVO checkpoints. These events, were they well known throughout the 306th Mountain Brigade? Did the soldiers in your brigade know about these events that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers in the 306th Brigade knew about these events that I have testified about today. Most of the soldiers knew about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as someone, sir, who was dealing with, among other things, morale of the soldiers within the 306th Mountain Brigade, can you tell us what effect these events had upon morale in the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the sector for moral guidance in the 306th Brigade worked a lot with soldiers from the 306th Brigade in order to raise the level of morale and to ensure they respected the level of conduct for BH Army soldiers. At meetings, we often told these soldiers how they should behave. We instructed them about the laws of war, and we told them about the conventions that had to be respected. So I think they were aware of these facts, and I believe that they didn't have revenge in their mind because of what had happened in Velika Bukovica, and this is confirmed by what I've already said, by the fact that when I was still an army member, no houses were destroyed or torched, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us just now as well as earlier this morning that you instructed them, or you said, "We instructed them about the laws of war and we told them about the conventions that had to be respected." When you say "we," "we told them about the laws of war," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I said quite specifically "we," the members of the sector for moral guidance. Husic Halim was my superior, there was myself, Jasarevic Ferid, and there was another person, Music Kasim, and Salim Tarakdzija. That was the team in the sector for moral guidance. So when I say "we," I'm referring to these members of the sector for moral guidance in the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber what specialised training you had in the laws of war or the conventions governing respect during war or armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't have any training, but I had sufficient information and I was sufficiently educated. What we knew at that time is what we would explain to those people. I did this along with my superior who was better educated than I was. This was done on the basis of my general knowledge and the knowledge I had obtained in the former JNA. And after the completion of one's military training, all able-bodied men had to join the reserve forces. We would be involved in such tasks for a few days. And when I was involved in training for the reserved forces, I also obtained such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That actually brings me to the next subject I wanted to ask you a couple of questions about. You told us earlier today - page 58, line 4 - that many of the soldiers in your brigade were not properly trained. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber a rough approximation, if you know, the approximate percentage of men who had at some point been in the JNA when the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still existed?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that there were between 60 and 70 per cent of men who had served in the former JNA that had certain military knowledge. This is a rough estimate. I assume that that would be a correct estimate, since I was a member of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about some of the work that you did during the period when you were involved in social services. You told us that among your duties was to provide food to families of soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We tried to make it possible through the civilian protection for the families of those soldiers to receive the necessary food while their sons were on the lines. But it's the logistics service that took care of the soldiers. So you have soldiers in units who go to positions, and then they receive food there. And on the other hand, you have the soldiers' families. We took care of the families of those soldiers, and we cooperated with the civilian authorities to take care of them. So these are two separate issues. This distinction has to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to understand what you're saying. You just told us "we tried to make it possible through the civilian protection for the families of those soldiers to receive the necessary food while their sons were on the lines." And my question, sir, is who provided the food? The army or the civilian protection? Or did the army give civilian protection foodstuffs for these civilian family members? How did this work?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, it functioned in the following manner: The army didn't provide the civilian protection with anything. There were humanitarian organisations that existed in Zenica, in Travnik. It was through these organisations that the civilian protection was furnished with certain supplies or certain food. And this was then given or distributed to civilians in a given area. And these civilians were naturally the families of soldiers who were at the lines. So the army didn't give anything to the civilian protection. The civilian protection would receive aid from humanitarian organisations present in the areas of Zenica and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you also told us earlier today that many of the Arabs in Mehurici originally were humanitarian workers. And later, some of them became, in effect, combatants. At the time period you were involved in social services, how many, if any, of the Arabs or Mujahedin in Mehurici were still involved in humanitarian work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would like to object to this question because the witness has quite clearly stated that in August 1993 he became involved in social affairs, and he spoke about the Arabs in 1992 and about their humanitarian work during that period of time and at another period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that in 1992, the Arabs were involved in humanitarian work. How long did that continue for? If you know.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, I said that they represented themselves, introduced themselves as being humanitarians and Arabs. And they really did from some stocks they had, I don't know where they got them from, they did give out quite a lot of assistance. There were a lot of poor inhabitants. How long that went on for, I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, from any time in the period when these Arabs arrived in the Mehurici area in late 1992 through mid-November 1993 when you returned to being a teacher, did you personally have any contact with any of these Arabs?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I did have personal contact with one Arab, and this is what it was about. In principle, we didn't contact with them or very rarely. But I personally was slightly afraid of those people. I didn't know them well enough. It was just the initial stages. I didn't know how to come into contact with them. But anyway, I met an Arab whose name was Ramadan, and this was in 1992. I can't remember the exact date or month. But there was an incident that happened, and it was this: While I was down there in the meeting room of our school building, we were doing some work there, and I heard that something was falling from the floor above, from the first floor, something fell down into the ground floor hallway. I got up to have a look, and they were books from my school, the school I work in now. They were regular reading books, compulsory reading books, and they were going to throw these books out and throw them into the river. I lost control. I am a man who has associated with books all my life, and I believe books to be the most important thing in life. I jumped up to protect the books belonging to my school. I went up to Ramadan and said, "Aren't you ashamed of what you are doing? Do you know? Do you realise? How would you feel if I went to your country and threw your books out? Threw your valuable books out, books that were a hundred years old?" And he said, "Well, these are communist books, they're not worth a penny." And I said, "That's not your affair. We're the ones who are going to determine which books are worth something and worth reading, which aren't. We'll do that after the war." And I told him not to do that any more. And he listened to me. He no longer threw them out. We took all the books up into the attic and stored them there, and once the war was over, we returned the books to their proper place, and many of them are on the compulsory reading list for students, for pupils. So that was the only contact I had with an Arab. Otherwise, I didn't have any direct contacts. I avoided them because in a way I suppose I was a bit afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a couple of questions about this incident with this person Ramadan. First of all, how did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew his name. He would move about in the building every day. He would go upstairs, and people would say, "That's Ramadan." And he was perhaps the person who moved around most. And people said his name was Ramadan. So when I saw him, I knew his name, called him out by name and told him what I told him. So I learned his name from others. He was the one that sort of moved around most and was most prominent perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, other than this name Ramadan, do you know the full name of this individual? His family name?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I knew nothing about the man. I think he came from Syria somewhere. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did this person, Ramadan, speak or understand the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: During this encounter with the book incident, he spoke, but spoke badly. He got his tenses wrong and his cases wrong, but you could sort of follow what he was saying. So he did speak, but he spoke badly, with a lot of mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, as a career educator in the Mehurici area, can you tell us approximately how many local Bosniaks in that area speak Arabic.

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. All I can say is that they spoke Arabic, people who had gone to university or studied in Arab countries or at the university in Sarajevo. I know Husic Halim, for example, he could speak Arabic. As to the others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the Arabic language taught in the primary school in Mehurici at any point in time during the 30-plus years you have been associated with that school?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, never. Arabic was never taught in our state schools. Arabic was never taught at school. What was taught during the socialist times was Russian. After that we moved to English. And in my school to this day, English is the language, the foreign language that is taught. We have very good teachers, highly qualified English teachers teaching our young people. So let me repeat: Arabic was never taught in our school, either during the war or before the war or indeed after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you have worked for a large number of years in the school in Mehurici. And I'm wondering if perhaps you know or can enlighten us as to how it came about that the school came to be used by the Arabs and then units of the Territorial Defence and later the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FERID JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I said at the beginning of my testimony that a part of the school building was used by the regional staff of Territorial Defence of Mehurici. And that was the command post for all our village units. So the regional staff of the Territorial Defence, later on, to grow into the 306th Brigade pursuant to some orders. Now, how the Arabs came to the school, I don't know. When I arrived one day, when I went home, they said that there were some people there up on the floor above, and that they were of Arab origin from Iraq and Iran. That's all I know. And later on I would see them. They would wear their national dress, their traditional costumes. So that's how it was. I don't know how they came to be there, who brought them there or anything else. But they were just there. They turned up there one day, but I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I've got just a few more questions. I don't know if you want me to continue, or if you would prefer that we adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you just have a few questions that take up a few minutes, and if the Defence have no further questions and if the Judges have no questions, perhaps we can make an effort and go on for a few more minutes to avoid having the witness-- but I see that you need more time. Right, Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not much time, but I would need between five and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, it would be more advisable to continue tomorrow. So we'll end there for the day. Sir, although we need 15 or 20 minutes, we will have to adjourn. We have to make a technical break for the day. And we reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Having said that, I hope that you won't be kept for too long tomorrow. And after this witness, we can get on with the next witness. So we reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
